chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.h: Bank P15 — Relative orbital motion near a circular target
chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Midterm 1 papers. Method: Notes §3.2 (velocity and acceleration in a moving frame), §4.9 (dynamics of relative motion, inertia forces) and §8.3 (circular orbits under the gravity of a point mass). The linearised equations obtained here are known as the Clohessy-Wiltshire (or Hill) equations: their use for rendezvous is an **extension** of the course, but every step uses only the course's tools. Every number was checked with SymPy, and the numerical case also with a nonlinear two-body integration.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
A target $T$ moves on a circular orbit of radius $R_T$ around the Earth, whose centre $O$ is the origin of the inertial frame $S_0$ and whose gravitational parameter is $\mu$ (the Earth's gravity on a mass $m$ at $\mathbf r$ is $-m\mu\,\mathbf r/|\mathbf r|^3$). The target's angular velocity is constant, $n\,\mathbf k$, with the **mean motion** $n=\sqrt{\mu/R_T^3}$ ($\mathbf k$ normal to the orbital plane). A chaser $P$ of mass $m$, subject only to the Earth's gravity, moves in the same plane close to $T$.

Use the frame $S_1=\{T;\mathbf e_x,\mathbf e_y,\mathbf k\}$ attached to the target: $\mathbf e_x$ radial, pointing away from $O$; $\mathbf e_y=\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_x$ along the target's velocity (along-track); $S_1$ rotates with $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}=n\,\mathbf k$. The relative position of the chaser is $\boldsymbol\rho=x\,\mathbf e_x+y\,\mathbf e_y$ with $|\boldsymbol\rho|\ll R_T$. Initial conditions at $t=0$: $x_0$, $y_0$, $\dot x_0$, $\dot y_0$ (relative to $S_1$).

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- Data: $\mu$, $R_T$, $n=\sqrt{\mu/R_T^3}$, the initial conditions. Numerical part (f): $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$, $R_T=6778$ km (low Earth orbit), chaser 1 km behind the target ($x_0=0$, $y_0=-1000$ m).
- Hypotheses: point masses, planar motion in the orbital plane, $S_0$ inertial, no drag, no other bodies; the target's orbit is not affected by the chaser; terms of order $|\boldsymbol\rho|^2/R_T^2$ are neglected in the gravity difference.
- The frame $S_1$ has a uniformly rotating basis ($\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}_{10}=\mathbf 0$) and an accelerated origin ($\mathbf a_T=-n^2R_T\,\mathbf e_x$).

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.h: (a) Degrees of freedom, frame and relative kinematics [1.5 pts]
chunks.x: How many degrees of freedom has $P$ in this planar problem? Write the absolute acceleration of $P$ in the basis of $S_1$ as the sum of the acceleration of $T$, the relative acceleration, the Coriolis and the centripetal terms, and list the inertia forces that act on $P$ in $S_1$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x: $\mathbf a_P=\mathbf a_T+\mathbf a_{rel}+2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)+\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho$, with $\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_x=\mathbf e_y$ and $\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_y=-\mathbf e_x$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- 2 degrees of freedom, $(x,y)$; $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}=n\mathbf k$ constant, $\mathbf a_T=-n^2R_T\,\mathbf e_x$.
- $\mathbf a_P=\big(-n^2R_T+\ddot x-2n\dot y-n^2x\big)\mathbf e_x+\big(\ddot y+2n\dot x-n^2y\big)\mathbf e_y$.
- Inertia forces in $S_1$: $-m\mathbf a_T=mn^2R_T\,\mathbf e_x$, centrifugal $mn^2\boldsymbol\rho$, Coriolis $-2mn\mathbf k\times\mathbf v_{rel}$; no Euler force.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Count

$P$ is free in the orbital plane: 2 degrees of freedom, the coordinates $(x,y)$ in $S_1$. There are no constraints and no reactions; the only force is gravity.

#### Step 2. Motion of the frame

$T$ moves on a circle of radius $R_T$ with constant angular velocity $n\mathbf k$, so its acceleration is purely centripetal: $\mathbf a_T=-n^2R_T\,\mathbf e_x$. The basis of $S_1$ turns with $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}=n\mathbf k$, and $\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}_{10}=\mathbf 0$.

Change of basis: take the inertial basis $\{\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\}$ of $S_0$ with $\mathbf i$ along $\overrightarrow{OT}$ at $t=0$. Then $\mathbf e_x=\cos nt\,\mathbf i+\sin nt\,\mathbf j$, $\mathbf e_y=\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_x=-\sin nt\,\mathbf i+\cos nt\,\mathbf j$, and

$$\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf e_x\\ \mathbf e_y\\ \mathbf k\end{pmatrix}=[R]\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf i\\ \mathbf j\\ \mathbf k\end{pmatrix},\qquad [R]=\begin{pmatrix}\cos nt&\sin nt&0\\ -\sin nt&\cos nt&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$$

The rows have length $\cos^2nt+\sin^2nt=1$, rows 1 and 2 are orthogonal ($-\cos nt\sin nt+\sin nt\cos nt=0$) and row 3 is $\mathbf k$, so $[R][R]^T=I$; $\det[R]=\cos^2nt+\sin^2nt=+1$. Differentiating, $\dot{\mathbf e}_x=n\,\mathbf e_y=n\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_x$ and $\dot{\mathbf e}_y=-n\,\mathbf e_x=n\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_y$ (Poisson), which confirms $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}=n\,\mathbf k$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 3. Relative kinematics

In $S_1$: $\mathbf v_{rel}=\dot x\,\mathbf e_x+\dot y\,\mathbf e_y$, $\mathbf a_{rel}=\ddot x\,\mathbf e_x+\ddot y\,\mathbf e_y$. With $\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_x=\mathbf e_y$, $\mathbf k\times\mathbf e_y=-\mathbf e_x$:

$$2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}=2n\big(\dot x\,\mathbf e_y-\dot y\,\mathbf e_x\big),\qquad \boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho=n\big(x\,\mathbf e_y-y\,\mathbf e_x\big),\qquad \boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)=-n^2\big(x\,\mathbf e_x+y\,\mathbf e_y\big)$$

The composition of accelerations (Notes §3.2), with the Euler term zero, gives

$$\mathbf a_P=\big(-n^2R_T+\ddot x-2n\dot y-n^2x\big)\,\mathbf e_x+\big(\ddot y+2n\dot x-n^2y\big)\,\mathbf e_y$$

#### Step 4. Inertia forces

Written as $m\mathbf a_{rel}=\mathbf F+\mathbf F_{in}$ (Notes §4.9), the inertia force is $\mathbf F_{in}=-m\mathbf a_T-2m\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}-m\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)$: the dragging force of the origin $mn^2R_T\,\mathbf e_x$, the centrifugal force $mn^2\boldsymbol\rho$ (about $T$) and the Coriolis force $-2mn\,\mathbf k\times\mathbf v_{rel}$. The Coriolis force is perpendicular to $\mathbf v_{rel}$ and does no work in $S_1$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.h: (b) Linearised gravity and the equations of motion [2.0 pts]
chunks.x: Expand the gravity on $P$ to first order in $|\boldsymbol\rho|/R_T$ and obtain the two equations of relative motion. Explain why the terms in $R_T$ disappear.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- $-\mu\,\mathbf r_P/|\mathbf r_P|^3\approx-n^2R_T\,\mathbf e_x+n^2\big(2x\,\mathbf e_x-y\,\mathbf e_y\big)$ (using $\mu=n^2R_T^3$).
- $\ddot x-2n\dot y-3n^2x=0$, $\qquad\ddot y+2n\dot x=0$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. The exact gravity

$\mathbf r_P=\overrightarrow{OT}+\boldsymbol\rho=(R_T+x)\,\mathbf e_x+y\,\mathbf e_y$ and $|\mathbf r_P|^2=R_T^2\big(1+\tfrac{2x}{R_T}+\tfrac{x^2+y^2}{R_T^2}\big)$.

#### Step 2. First-order expansion

Keeping only first-order terms, $u=2x/R_T$ and $(1+u)^{-3/2}=1-\tfrac32u+O(u^2)$:

$$\frac1{|\mathbf r_P|^3}\approx\frac1{R_T^3}\Big(1-\frac{3x}{R_T}\Big)$$

$$-\frac{\mu\,\mathbf r_P}{|\mathbf r_P|^3}\approx-\frac{\mu}{R_T^3}\Big(1-\frac{3x}{R_T}\Big)\big[(R_T+x)\,\mathbf e_x+y\,\mathbf e_y\big]\approx-\frac{\mu}{R_T^2}\,\mathbf e_x+\frac{\mu}{R_T^3}\big(2x\,\mathbf e_x-y\,\mathbf e_y\big)$$

(the product $x\cdot3x/R_T$ and $y\cdot3x/R_T$ are second order and dropped). The circular orbit of $T$ gives $n^2R_T=\mu/R_T^2$ (Notes §8.3), i.e. $\mu/R_T^3=n^2$.

#### Step 3. Newton in $S_0$, projected on the basis of $S_1$

$m\mathbf a_P=-m\mu\mathbf r_P/|\mathbf r_P|^3$ with $\mathbf a_P$ of (a):

$$\mathbf e_x:\quad -n^2R_T+\ddot x-2n\dot y-n^2x=-n^2R_T+2n^2x$$

$$\mathbf e_y:\quad \ddot y+2n\dot x-n^2y=-n^2y$$

The terms $-n^2R_T$ cancel: the gravity at $T$ is exactly what keeps $T$ (and $S_1$) on its orbit, so only the **difference** of gravity between $P$ and $T$ (the tidal term) drives the relative motion. Likewise the centrifugal term $-n^2y$ cancels the along-track gravity component. Hence

$$\ddot x-2n\dot y-3n^2x=0,\qquad \ddot y+2n\dot x=0$$

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x: The second equation is an exact derivative: $\frac{d}{dt}(\dot y+2nx)=0$. Substitute in the first to obtain a harmonic oscillator with a constant forcing; then integrate $\dot y$ with Barrow's rule.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- First integral $\dot y+2nx=C\equiv\dot y_0+2nx_0$; then $\ddot x+n^2x=2nC$.
- $x(t)=4x_0+\dfrac{2\dot y_0}{n}-\Big(3x_0+\dfrac{2\dot y_0}{n}\Big)\cos nt+\dfrac{\dot x_0}{n}\sin nt$.
- $y(t)=y_0-(6nx_0+3\dot y_0)\,t+\Big(6x_0+\dfrac{4\dot y_0}{n}\Big)\sin nt+\dfrac{2\dot x_0}{n}(\cos nt-1)$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. First integral

$\ddot y+2n\dot x=\frac{d}{dt}\big(\dot y+2nx\big)=0$. Integrating from $0$ to $t$ (Barrow): $\big[\dot y+2nx\big]_0^t=0$, so

$$\dot y+2nx=C,\qquad C=\dot y_0+2nx_0$$

#### Step 2. Radial equation

Substitute $\dot y=C-2nx$ in the radial equation: $\ddot x-2n(C-2nx)-3n^2x=0$, i.e.

$$\ddot x+n^2x=2nC$$

A particular solution is the constant $x_p=2C/n$; the homogeneous solution is $A\cos nt+B\sin nt$. The initial conditions give $x(0)=2C/n+A=x_0$ and $\dot x(0)=nB=\dot x_0$:

$$A=x_0-\frac{2C}{n}=-3x_0-\frac{2\dot y_0}{n},\qquad B=\frac{\dot x_0}{n}$$

$$x(t)=4x_0+\frac{2\dot y_0}{n}-\Big(3x_0+\frac{2\dot y_0}{n}\Big)\cos nt+\frac{\dot x_0}{n}\sin nt$$

#### Step 3. Along-track position

From Step 1, $\dot y=C-2nx=-3C-2nA\cos nt-2nB\sin nt$. Integrating from $0$ to $t$ with the antiderivatives $\int\cos n\tau\,d\tau=\frac{\sin n\tau}{n}$ and $\int\sin n\tau\,d\tau=-\frac{\cos n\tau}{n}$ (chain rule: $\frac{d}{d\tau}\sin n\tau=n\cos n\tau$) and Barrow's rule:

$$y(t)-y_0=-3Ct-2nA\Big[\frac{\sin n\tau}{n}\Big]_0^t-2nB\Big[-\frac{\cos n\tau}{n}\Big]_0^t=-3Ct-2A\sin nt+2B(\cos nt-1)$$

With $C$, $A$, $B$:

$$y(t)=y_0-(6nx_0+3\dot y_0)\,t+\Big(6x_0+\frac{4\dot y_0}{n}\Big)\sin nt+\frac{2\dot x_0}{n}(\cos nt-1)$$

Check: $x(0)=x_0$, $y(0)=y_0$, $\dot x(0)=\dot x_0$, $\dot y(0)=-6nx_0-3\dot y_0+6nx_0+4\dot y_0=\dot y_0$.

chunks.h: (d) Secular drift: the trap of the lower orbit [1.5 pts]
chunks.x: Find the along-track drift per orbit and the condition for no drift. A chaser is placed 1 km **below** the target on its **own circular orbit** (radius $R_T-1$ km): does it keep its position below $T$? Compare with a chaser released 1 km below $T$ at rest in $S_1$.

chunks.x: Only the term proportional to $t$ grows. For the circular orbit of radius $R_T+x_0$, $\dot y_0=(R_T+x_0)(n'-n)$ with $n'=\sqrt{\mu/(R_T+x_0)^3}$; expand to first order.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- $\Delta y_{orbit}=-\dfrac{2\pi}{n}\,(6nx_0+3\dot y_0)=-12\pi x_0-\dfrac{6\pi\dot y_0}{n}$; no drift iff $\dot y_0=-2nx_0$ (i.e. $C=0$).
- Own circular orbit: $\dot y_0\approx-\tfrac32nx_0$, $x\equiv x_0$, $\Delta y_{orbit}=-3\pi x_0=+9.42$ km per orbit for $x_0=-1$ km: it **moves ahead** of $T$.
- At rest in $S_1$ ($\dot y_0=0$): $\Delta y_{orbit}=-12\pi x_0=+37.70$ km per orbit.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Drift per orbit

The periodic terms of $y(t)$ repeat after one orbital period $2\pi/n$, and $x(2\pi/n)=x_0$; only the secular term changes:

$$\Delta y_{orbit}=y\Big(\frac{2\pi}n\Big)-y_0=-(6nx_0+3\dot y_0)\,\frac{2\pi}{n}=-12\pi x_0-\frac{6\pi\,\dot y_0}{n}$$

It vanishes iff $6nx_0+3\dot y_0=0$:

$$\dot y_0=-2n\,x_0\quad(C=0)$$

#### Step 2. Chaser on its own circular orbit

The circular orbit of radius $R_T+x_0$ has angular rate $n'=\sqrt{\mu/(R_T+x_0)^3}=n\,(1+x_0/R_T)^{-3/2}\approx n\big(1-\tfrac{3x_0}{2R_T}\big)$. Its velocity in $S_1$ is the absolute velocity minus the transport velocity $n\mathbf k\times\mathbf r$: $\dot y_0=(R_T+x_0)(n'-n)\approx R_T\cdot n\cdot\big(-\tfrac{3x_0}{2R_T}\big)=-\tfrac32nx_0$ (first order). Then $C=\tfrac12nx_0$, $A=-3x_0+3x_0=0$, so $x(t)=x_0$ for all $t$ and

$$y(t)=y_0-\tfrac32n\,x_0\,t,\qquad \Delta y_{orbit}=-3\pi x_0$$

For $x_0=-1000$ m: $\Delta y_{orbit}=+3000\pi=+9425$ m per orbit. **The trap:** "same circular motion, so it stays below" is wrong. The lower orbit has a shorter period (Kepler), so the chaser moves ahead of the target at $\tfrac32n|x_0|$. The no-drift value $-2nx_0$ is **not** the circular-orbit value $-\tfrac32nx_0$: the drift-free relative motion is the ellipse of (e), not a fixed point.

#### Step 3. Chaser at rest in $S_1$

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x: With $\dot y_0=0$ (and $\dot x_0=0$): $\Delta y_{orbit}=-12\pi x_0=+12\,000\pi$ m $=+37.70$ km per orbit, while $x$ oscillates between $x_0$ and $7x_0$ ($x(t)=4x_0-3x_0\cos nt$, i.e. down to 7 km below $T$): a point "at rest" below the target is moving slower than the local circular speed and falls into an eccentric orbit.

chunks.x: For $\dot y_0=-2nx_0$, show that the relative trajectory is an ellipse centred on the along-track axis, with the along-track semi-axis twice the radial one. Find its centre, its period and its sense of motion.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- $x=x_0\cos nt+\dfrac{\dot x_0}{n}\sin nt$, $\ y=y_c-2x_0\sin nt+\dfrac{2\dot x_0}{n}\cos nt$, $\ y_c=y_0-\dfrac{2\dot x_0}{n}$.
- $\dfrac{x^2}{A_e^2}+\dfrac{(y-y_c)^2}{4A_e^2}=1$, $A_e=\sqrt{x_0^2+\dot x_0^2/n^2}$; period $2\pi/n$; run in the sense of $-\mathbf k$ (opposite to the orbital motion).

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Substitution

With $\dot y_0=-2nx_0$: $4x_0+2\dot y_0/n=0$, $3x_0+2\dot y_0/n=-x_0$, $6nx_0+3\dot y_0=0$ and $6x_0+4\dot y_0/n=-2x_0$. Then (c) gives

$$x=x_0\cos nt+\frac{\dot x_0}{n}\sin nt,\qquad y=y_0-\frac{2\dot x_0}{n}-2x_0\sin nt+\frac{2\dot x_0}{n}\cos nt$$

#### Step 2. The ellipse

With $A_e\cos\delta=x_0$, $A_e\sin\delta=\dot x_0/n$ and the addition formulas, $x=A_e\cos(nt-\delta)$ and $y-y_c=-2\big(x_0\sin nt-\tfrac{\dot x_0}{n}\cos nt\big)=-2A_e\sin(nt-\delta)$. Using $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$:

$$\frac{x^2}{A_e^2}+\frac{(y-y_c)^2}{4A_e^2}=1$$

an ellipse centred at $(0,y_c)$, with semi-axes $A_e$ (radial) and $2A_e$ (along-track), run once per orbital period $2\pi/n$.

#### Step 3. Sense of motion

The $\mathbf k$-component of $\big(x\,\mathbf e_x+(y-y_c)\,\mathbf e_y\big)\times\big(\dot x\,\mathbf e_x+\dot y\,\mathbf e_y\big)$ is $x\dot y-(y-y_c)\dot x=A_e\cos\theta\,(-2A_en\cos\theta)-(-2A_e\sin\theta)(-A_en\sin\theta)=-2nA_e^2<0$ (with $\theta=nt-\delta$): the ellipse is run in the sense of $-\mathbf k$. Above the target ($x>0$) the chaser moves backwards ($\dot y<0$), below it moves forwards: higher means slower.

chunks.h: (f) A low Earth orbit case: two manoeuvres [1.5 pts]
chunks.x: Data: $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$, $R_T=6778$ km; the chaser is 1 km behind the target, $x_0=0$, $y_0=-1000$ m, at rest in $S_1$, and receives an impulse at $t=0$. (i) The impulse is radial, $\dot x_0=+0.5$ m/s. Describe the motion and give the position after half an orbit and after one orbit. (ii) Which **along-track** impulse $\dot y_0$ (with $\dot x_0=0$) brings the chaser onto the target after exactly one orbit? Which way does it point, how far does the chaser go from the orbit, and with what relative velocity does it arrive?

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- $n=1.1314\times10^{-3}$ rad/s, period $2\pi/n=5553$ s $=92.6$ min.
- (i) $C=0$: bounded ellipse with $A_e=\dot x_0/n=441.9$ m, centre $y_c=-1884$ m; at half orbit $(x,y)=(0,-2768$ m$)$; after one orbit back at $(0,-1000$ m$)$: no gain.
- (ii) $\dot y_0=\dfrac{y_0\,n}{6\pi}=\dfrac{y_0}{3\cdot2\pi/n}=-0.0600$ m/s (**backwards**); $x$ reaches $4\dot y_0/n=-212.2$ m at half orbit; arrival with $\mathbf v_{rel}=\dot y_0\,\mathbf e_y$, so a braking impulse of $+0.0600$ m/s is needed. A nonlinear two-body integration misses the target by about 3 m (2.8 m).

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Mean motion

$$n=\sqrt{\frac{3.986\times10^{14}}{(6.778\times10^6)^3}}=1.1314\times10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1},\qquad \frac{2\pi}{n}=5553\ \text{s}=92.6\ \text{min}$$

#### Step 2. Radial impulse

$x_0=0$, $\dot y_0=0$: $C=\dot y_0+2nx_0=0$, so the motion is the bounded ellipse of (e), with $A_e=\dot x_0/n=0.5/1.1314\times10^{-3}=441.9$ m:

$$x=441.9\,\sin nt\ \text{m},\qquad y=-1000+883.9\,(\cos nt-1)\ \text{m}$$

At half an orbit ($nt=\pi$): $x=0$, $y=-1000-4\cdot441.9=-2768$ m (the chaser rose and fell behind); centre of the ellipse $y_c=y_0-2\dot x_0/n=-1884$ m. After one orbit it is back at $(0,-1000)$ m: a radial impulse alone gains nothing.

#### Step 3. Along-track impulse for a one-orbit rendezvous

With $x_0=\dot x_0=0$, (c) gives $x=\frac{2\dot y_0}{n}(1-\cos nt)$ and $y=y_0-3\dot y_0t+\frac{4\dot y_0}{n}\sin nt$. At $t=2\pi/n$, $\sin2\pi=0$, $\cos2\pi=1$: $x=0$ and

$$0=y_0-3\dot y_0\,\frac{2\pi}{n}\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot y_0=\frac{y_0\,n}{6\pi}=\frac{-1000}{3\cdot5553}=-0.0600\ \text{m/s}$$

**The trap:** to catch a target 1 km **ahead**, the chaser must thrust **backwards**. The backward impulse lowers its orbit ($x$ reaches $\frac{4\dot y_0}{n}=-212.2$ m at half orbit), and the lower orbit is faster, so it gains $3|\dot y_0|\cdot2\pi/n=1000$ m in one period. A forward impulse would raise the chaser and make it fall behind.

#### Step 4. Arrival

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x: At $t=2\pi/n$: $\dot x=2\dot y_0\sin nt=0$ and $\dot y=-3\dot y_0+4\dot y_0\cos nt=\dot y_0$. The chaser arrives at $T$ with $\mathbf v_{rel}=-0.0600\,\mathbf e_y$ m/s, so a second impulse of $+0.0600$ m/s along $\mathbf e_y$ stops it at the target (total $0.120$ m/s). A numerical integration of the full nonlinear two-body equations from the same initial state misses the target by about 3 m (2.8 m) after one orbit, consistent with neglecting terms of order $|\boldsymbol\rho|^2/R_T$.

chunks.t: Relative orbital motion near a target on a circular orbit: Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, drift and a counter-i
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** $n$ is s$^{-1}$ ($\mu/R^3$ is m$^3$s$^{-2}$/m$^3$); every term of $\ddot x-2n\dot y-3n^2x$ is m s$^{-2}$; $\dot y_0/n$ is m, so $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are m; $\Delta y_{orbit}=-12\pi x_0-6\pi\dot y_0/n$ is m.
- **Limiting cases:** $\boldsymbol\rho=\mathbf 0$ with zero relative velocity stays at the origin (the target itself). $n\to0$ (no gravity, non-rotating frame): expanding $\cos nt\approx1-\tfrac12n^2t^2$ and $\sin nt\approx nt-\tfrac16n^3t^3$ in (c) gives $x\to x_0+\dot x_0t$, $y\to y_0+\dot y_0t$, uniform straight motion, as it must.
- **Physical meaning of $C$:** $C=\dot y+2nx$ is constant; it measures the difference of orbital period between chaser and target (to first order the chaser's semi-major axis differs from $R_T$ by $2C/n$). Equal periods ($C=0$) means no drift; that is why the radial impulse of (f)(i) gives a closed loop.
- **Common mistakes in the exam:** (1) forgetting the acceleration of the origin $\mathbf a_T$ or the centrifugal term, which leaves an $R_T$ term that does not cancel; (2) expanding $|\mathbf r_P|^{-3}$ with the wrong exponent ($1-2x/R_T$ instead of $1-3x/R_T$); (3) assuming that a chaser below the target on its own circular orbit, or at rest in $S_1$, keeps its relative position; (4) thrusting towards the target to catch it.

chunks.x:
Practice item, not an official exercise
Written for the bank in the style of the Midterm 1 papers. Method: Notes §6.4 and §6.5 (constraint forces, their power, dynamical decoupling), §3.2 and §4.9 (motion relative to a translating frame), §4.5 (mechanical energy) and the linear momentum theorem for a system of particles. Every number was checked with SymPy.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x: A wedge of mass $M$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. Its upper face is a smooth plane inclined at the angle $\alpha$ ($0<\alpha<\pi/2$) to the horizontal, descending towards $-x$; the top edge is $A$ and the corner of the wedge under $A$ is $B$. A particle $P$ of mass $m$ is placed on the incline. The inertial frame is $S_0=\{O;\mathbf i,\mathbf j\}$ ($x$ horizontal, $y$ vertical upwards, gravity $-g\,\mathbf j$). The wedge translates without rotating (it does not tip), and its position is the abscissa $X$ of $B$. The position of $P$ on the incline is the distance $s=|AP|$ measured from $A$ **down the slope**, along the unit vector $\mathbf u=-\cos\alpha\,\mathbf i-\sin\alpha\,\mathbf j$; $\mathbf n=-\sin\alpha\,\mathbf i+\cos\alpha\,\mathbf j$ is the unit normal of the incline pointing out of the wedge. Both bodies are released from rest at $t=0$ with $s=0$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- Data: $m$, $M$, $\alpha$, $g$. Numerical parts: $\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$, and the particle has slid a distance $L$ along the incline.
- Hypotheses: point particle, rigid wedge translating on the table, all contacts smooth (no friction), $S_0$ inertial; the contact of $P$ with the incline is unilateral ($N\ge0$, checked in (d)).
- Frames: $S_0$ and the frame $S_1=\{A;\mathbf n,\mathbf u\}$ attached to the wedge, ordered so that it is right-handed: $\mathbf n\times\mathbf u=\big[(-\sin\alpha)(-\sin\alpha)-\cos\alpha\,(-\cos\alpha)\big]\mathbf k=\mathbf k$ (the order $\{\mathbf u,\mathbf n\}$ would give $\mathbf u\times\mathbf n=-\mathbf k$, a left-handed basis). $S_1$ **translates** with acceleration $\ddot X\,\mathbf i$ and does not rotate.
- Basis change: $\mathbf i=-\sin\alpha\,\mathbf n-\cos\alpha\,\mathbf u$, $\ \mathbf j=\cos\alpha\,\mathbf n-\sin\alpha\,\mathbf u$ (from $\mathbf i\cdot\mathbf n=-\sin\alpha$, $\mathbf i\cdot\mathbf u=-\cos\alpha$, $\mathbf j\cdot\mathbf n=\cos\alpha$, $\mathbf j\cdot\mathbf u=-\sin\alpha$).

In matrix form:

$$\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf i\\ \mathbf j\end{pmatrix}=[R]\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf n\\ \mathbf u\end{pmatrix},\qquad [R]=\begin{pmatrix}-\sin\alpha & -\cos\alpha\\ \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha\end{pmatrix}$$

chunks.x: with $[R][R]^T=\begin{pmatrix}\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha & -\sin\alpha\cos\alpha+\cos\alpha\sin\alpha\\ -\sin\alpha\cos\alpha+\cos\alpha\sin\alpha & \cos^2\alpha+\sin^2\alpha\end{pmatrix}=I$ and $\det[R]=\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha=+1$.

chunks.h: (a) Degrees of freedom and constraints [1.0 pts]
chunks.x: How many degrees of freedom has the system particle + wedge? Classify the constraint that keeps $P$ on the incline, as seen in $S_0$ and in $S_1$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- 2 degrees of freedom, $(X,s)$.
- $P$ on the incline: holonomic, unilateral, smooth; scleronomic as a relation between the coordinates $(X,s)$ of the system (no explicit $t$); it would be rheonomic for $P$ alone only if $X(t)$ were a prescribed function of time, which it is not here.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Count

The wedge is a rigid body in the plane (3 coordinates); the table fixes its height and, since it does not tip, its orientation: 1 coordinate $X$ remains. The particle has 2 coordinates in the plane; staying on the incline removes one, leaving $s$. In total **2 degrees of freedom**, $(X,s)$. Unlike a fixed incline, $X(t)$ is an unknown: the motion of the support depends on the motion of the particle.

#### Step 2. Classification

The condition "$P$ on the incline" reads $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\mathbf n=0$, i.e. $-(x_P-X)\sin\alpha+(y_P-h)\cos\alpha=0$ with $\overrightarrow{OA}=X\,\mathbf i+h\,\mathbf j$, a relation between the positions of $P$ and of the wedge: it is **holonomic** and, written in the system coordinates $(X,s)$ (or $(X,x_P,y_P)$), it contains no explicit time, so it is **scleronomic**. It would be rheonomic for $P$ alone only if the motion $X(t)$ of the wedge were prescribed from outside; here $X$ is an unknown, so the time enters only through the coordinates. In $S_1$ the plane is fixed. It is **unilateral**: $P$ can leave the plane upwards, so it holds only while $N\ge0$. Smooth: the reaction is $\mathbf N=N\,\mathbf n$, with no component along $\mathbf u$ (Notes §6.4).

chunks.x: $S_1$ does not rotate, so $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_A+\mathbf v_{rel}$ and $\mathbf a_P=\mathbf a_A+\mathbf a_{rel}$ with $\mathbf a_A=\ddot X\,\mathbf i$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- $\mathbf r_{rel}=s\,\mathbf u$, $\ \mathbf v_{rel}=\dot s\,\mathbf u$, $\ \mathbf a_{rel}=\ddot s\,\mathbf u$.
- $\mathbf a_P=\ddot X\,\mathbf i+\ddot s\,\mathbf u=(\ddot s-\ddot X\cos\alpha)\,\mathbf u-\ddot X\sin\alpha\,\mathbf n$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Relative motion

$\mathbf u$ is fixed in $S_1$, so $\mathbf r_{rel}=\overrightarrow{AP}=s\,\mathbf u$, $\ \mathbf v_{rel}=\dot s\,\mathbf u$, $\ \mathbf a_{rel}=\ddot s\,\mathbf u$. The relative velocity is tangent to the incline.

#### Step 2. Absolute motion

$\overrightarrow{OA}=X\,\mathbf i+h\,\mathbf j$ with the height $h$ of the wedge constant, so $\mathbf v_A=\dot X\,\mathbf i$, $\mathbf a_A=\ddot X\,\mathbf i$. Since $\boldsymbol\omega_{10}=\mathbf 0$ (Notes §3.2):

$$\mathbf v_P=\dot X\,\mathbf i+\dot s\,\mathbf u,\qquad \mathbf a_P=\ddot X\,\mathbf i+\ddot s\,\mathbf u$$

Substituting $\mathbf i=-\cos\alpha\,\mathbf u-\sin\alpha\,\mathbf n$:

$$\mathbf a_P=(\ddot s-\ddot X\cos\alpha)\,\mathbf u-\ddot X\sin\alpha\,\mathbf n$$

and in Cartesian components $\mathbf v_P=(\dot X-\dot s\cos\alpha)\,\mathbf i-\dot s\sin\alpha\,\mathbf j$.

chunks.x: Write the forces on $P$ in $S_1$, including the inertia force, and on the wedge. Obtain $\ddot X$, $\ddot s$ and $N$, and the reaction of the table on the wedge.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x: Project $m\mathbf a_{rel}=\mathbf W+\mathbf N+\mathbf F_{in}$ on $\mathbf u$ (no $N$) and on $\mathbf n$. The wedge receives $-\mathbf N$ (action and reaction); its horizontal equation closes the system.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- $\ddot s=g\sin\alpha+\ddot X\cos\alpha$, $\ N=m(g\cos\alpha-\ddot X\sin\alpha)$, $\ M\ddot X=N\sin\alpha$.
- $\ddot X=\dfrac{m\,g\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$, $\ \ddot s=\dfrac{(M+m)\,g\sin\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$, $\ N=\dfrac{M\,m\,g\cos\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$.
- Table reaction $R=Mg+N\cos\alpha$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Forces on $P$ in $S_1$

Weight $\mathbf W=-mg\,\mathbf j=mg\sin\alpha\,\mathbf u-mg\cos\alpha\,\mathbf n$; reaction $\mathbf N=N\,\mathbf n$; inertia force of the translating frame (Notes §4.9) $\mathbf F_{in}=-m\,\mathbf a_A=-m\ddot X\,\mathbf i=m\ddot X\cos\alpha\,\mathbf u+m\ddot X\sin\alpha\,\mathbf n$. There is no Coriolis or centrifugal force ($\boldsymbol\omega_{10}=\mathbf 0$).

#### Step 2. Projections for $P$

$m\,\ddot s\,\mathbf u=\mathbf W+\mathbf N+\mathbf F_{in}$:

$$\mathbf u:\quad m\ddot s=mg\sin\alpha+m\ddot X\cos\alpha\ \Longrightarrow\ \ddot s=g\sin\alpha+\ddot X\cos\alpha$$

$$\mathbf n:\quad 0=-mg\cos\alpha+N+m\ddot X\sin\alpha\ \Longrightarrow\ N=m\big(g\cos\alpha-\ddot X\sin\alpha\big)$$

The $\mathbf u$ equation is free of the reaction (dynamical decoupling, Notes §6.5), but it still contains the unknown $\ddot X$.

#### Step 3. The wedge

Forces on the wedge: its weight $-Mg\,\mathbf j$, the table reaction $R\,\mathbf j$ (smooth table, vertical) and $-\mathbf N=-N\mathbf n=N\sin\alpha\,\mathbf i-N\cos\alpha\,\mathbf j$. Newton for the translating wedge, $M\ddot X\,\mathbf i=-Mg\,\mathbf j+R\,\mathbf j-N\mathbf n$:

$$\mathbf i:\quad M\ddot X=N\sin\alpha,\qquad \mathbf j:\quad 0=R-Mg-N\cos\alpha$$

#### Step 4. Solve

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
Substituting $N$ of Step 2 in the wedge equation: $M\ddot X=m\sin\alpha\,(g\cos\alpha-\ddot X\sin\alpha)$, so $\ddot X\,(M+m\sin^2\alpha)=m\,g\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$:

$$\ddot X=\frac{m\,g\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$$

Then, with $\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha=1$:

$$\ddot s=g\sin\alpha+\frac{m\,g\sin\alpha\cos^2\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}=\frac{g\sin\alpha\,(M+m\sin^2\alpha+m\cos^2\alpha)}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}=\frac{(M+m)\,g\sin\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$$

$$N=mg\cos\alpha-\frac{m^2g\sin^2\alpha\cos\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}=\frac{M\,m\,g\cos\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$$

and $R=Mg+N\cos\alpha$. All three accelerations are **constant**. Check with the system: the vertical external forces are $R-(M+m)g=N\cos\alpha-mg$, which equals $m\,\mathbf a_P\cdot\mathbf j=-m\ddot s\sin\alpha$ (the wedge has no vertical acceleration). An independent check with the Lagrange equations in $(X,s)$ gives the same $\ddot X$ and $\ddot s$.

#### Step 5. Numbers ($\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$)

$M+m\sin^2\alpha=2m+m/4=\tfrac94m$: $\ \ddot X=\dfrac{mg\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2}{\frac94m}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{9}g=0.1925\,g$, $\ \ddot s=\dfrac{3m\,g\cdot\frac12}{\frac94m}=\dfrac23g$, $\ N=\dfrac{2m\cdot m\,g\frac{\sqrt3}2}{\frac94m}=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{9}mg=0.7698\,mg$ (smaller than $mg\cos30^\circ=0.866\,mg$ on a fixed wedge).

chunks.h: (d) Limits, the sign of $N$ and the massless wedge [1.5 pts]
chunks.x: Check that $N>0$ for every $M>0$. Study the limits $M\to\infty$ and $M\to0$. In the second one a student says: "the particle slides down a plane, so it accelerates along the incline with $g\sin\alpha$ times some factor and presses on it". Discuss.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- $N>0$ for $M>0$ and $0<\alpha<\pi/2$: the particle never leaves the incline; $R>Mg>0$.
- $M\to\infty$: $\ddot X\to0$, $\ddot s\to g\sin\alpha$, $N\to mg\cos\alpha$ (fixed incline).
- $M\to0$: $N\to0$, $\ddot X\to g\cot\alpha$, $\ddot s\to g/\sin\alpha$ and $\mathbf a_P\to-g\,\mathbf j$: **free fall**; the massless wedge is pushed away just fast enough to stay in contact without force.
- The factor $\ddot s/(g\sin\alpha)=(M+m)/(M+m\sin^2\alpha)\ge1$ grows to $1/\sin^2\alpha$ as $M\to0$; the student's error is "presses on the wedge", since $N\to0$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Sign of the reaction

$N=\dfrac{Mmg\cos\alpha}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$: numerator and denominator are positive for $M>0$ and $0<\alpha<\pi/2$, so $N>0$ throughout the motion (the accelerations are constant, so $N$ is too). The unilateral constraint is never violated, and $R=Mg+N\cos\alpha>Mg>0$: the wedge stays on the table.

#### Step 2. Heavy wedge

Dividing numerator and denominator by $M$ and letting $M\to\infty$ ($m/M\to0$): $\ddot X\to0$, $\ddot s\to g\sin\alpha$, $N\to mg\cos\alpha$, the results of a fixed incline.

#### Step 3. Massless wedge (the trap)

Setting $M=0$: $N\to0$, $\ddot X\to\dfrac{mg\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{m\sin^2\alpha}=g\cot\alpha$, $\ddot s\to\dfrac{mg\sin\alpha}{m\sin^2\alpha}=\dfrac{g}{\sin\alpha}$. The absolute acceleration is

$$\mathbf a_P=g\cot\alpha\,\mathbf i+\frac{g}{\sin\alpha}\big(-\cos\alpha\,\mathbf i-\sin\alpha\,\mathbf j\big)=-g\,\mathbf j$$

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x: The particle **falls freely**; the incline exerts no force on it. A massless wedge cannot push back ($M\ddot X=N\sin\alpha$ with $M=0$ forces $N=0$), so it flies away horizontally with $g\cot\alpha$, exactly the motion that keeps the surface under the falling particle. The first half of the student's statement is harmless: $\ddot s=g\sin\alpha\cdot\dfrac{M+m}{M+m\sin^2\alpha}$ is indeed $g\sin\alpha$ times a factor, and this factor is $\ge1$ for every $M$ (because $M+m\ge M+m\sin^2\alpha$), growing from $1$ ($M\to\infty$) to $1/\sin^2\alpha$ ($M\to0$), which gives $\ddot s\to g/\sin\alpha$. The error is the second half, "the particle presses on the wedge": $N\to0$, the incline exerts no force and the particle is in free fall, merely accompanied by the surface.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.h: (e) First integrals and the speeds after sliding a distance $L$ [2.0 pts]
chunks.x: Show that the horizontal linear momentum of the system and its mechanical energy are conserved, explaining why the reaction $\mathbf N$ does no net work although it works on each body. For $\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$, find $\dot s$, $\dot X$ and $|\mathbf v_P|$ when $P$ has slid a distance $L$, and the work of $\mathbf N$ on $P$ and on the wedge.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x: The external forces on the system (weights, table reaction) are vertical. The power of $\mathbf N$ on $P$ plus that of $-\mathbf N$ on the wedge is $\mathbf N\cdot(\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_A)=\mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_{rel}$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- $p_x=M\dot X+m(\dot X-\dot s\cos\alpha)=0\Rightarrow\dot X=\dfrac{m\cos\alpha}{M+m}\,\dot s$; $\ \tfrac12M\dot X^2+\tfrac12m|\mathbf v_P|^2-mgs\sin\alpha=0$.
- $\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$: $E_{kin}=\tfrac38m\dot s^2$, $\dot s^2=\tfrac43gL$ ($\dot s=1.1547\sqrt{gL}$), $\dot X=\tfrac13\sqrt{gL}$, $|\mathbf v_P|=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{3}\sqrt{gL}=0.8819\sqrt{gL}$.
- Work of $\mathbf N$ on $P$: $-\tfrac19mgL$; on the wedge: $+\tfrac19mgL$; total 0.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. Horizontal momentum

The external forces on the system $\{P,\text{wedge}\}$ are $-mg\,\mathbf j$, $-Mg\,\mathbf j$ and $R\,\mathbf j$: no horizontal component. $\mathbf N$ is internal (action-reaction pair). The linear momentum theorem gives $\frac{d}{dt}p_x=0$, with $p_x=M\dot X+m\,\mathbf v_P\cdot\mathbf i=M\dot X+m(\dot X-\dot s\cos\alpha)$. From rest, $p_x=0$:

$$\dot X=\frac{m\cos\alpha}{M+m}\,\dot s$$

Consequently the centre of mass has $\ddot x_G=0$ and moves only vertically.

#### Step 2. Energy

Powers: the weights are conservative; $R\,\mathbf j\cdot\dot X\,\mathbf i=0$; the pair $\mathbf N$, $-\mathbf N$ has total power

$$\mathbf N\cdot\mathbf v_P+(-\mathbf N)\cdot\mathbf v_A=\mathbf N\cdot(\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_A)=N\,\mathbf n\cdot\dot s\,\mathbf u=0$$

because the relative velocity is tangent to the smooth incline (Notes §6.4). So the mechanical energy of the system is constant (Notes §4.5). With the zero of potential energy at $s=0$, the height of $P$ changes by $-s\sin\alpha$:

$$\tfrac12M\dot X^2+\tfrac12m\big[(\dot X-\dot s\cos\alpha)^2+\dot s^2\sin^2\alpha\big]-mg\,s\sin\alpha=0$$

#### Step 3. Kinetic energy for $\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
$\dot X=\frac{m\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2}{3m}\,\dot s=\frac{\sqrt3}{6}\,\dot s$. For $P$: $\dot X-\dot s\cos\alpha=\big(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}-\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{6}\big)\dot s=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\dot s$, whose square is $\tfrac13\dot s^2$, and $\dot s^2\sin^2\alpha=\tfrac14\dot s^2$, so $|\mathbf v_P|^2=\tfrac7{12}\dot s^2$ and $\tfrac12m|\mathbf v_P|^2=\tfrac7{24}m\dot s^2$. For the wedge: $\dot X^2=\tfrac3{36}\dot s^2=\tfrac1{12}\dot s^2$ and $\tfrac12(2m)\tfrac1{12}\dot s^2=\tfrac2{24}m\dot s^2$. Total:

$$E_{kin}=\frac{2+7}{24}\,m\dot s^2=\frac38\,m\dot s^2$$

#### Step 4. Speeds after sliding $L$

With $s=L$ and $mgL\sin30^\circ=\tfrac12mgL$:

$$\tfrac38m\dot s^2=\tfrac12mgL\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot s^2=\tfrac43gL,\quad \dot s=1.1547\sqrt{gL},\quad \dot X=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}\cdot\tfrac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{gL}=\tfrac13\sqrt{gL}$$

$$|\mathbf v_P|^2=\tfrac7{12}\cdot\tfrac43gL=\tfrac79gL,\qquad |\mathbf v_P|=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{3}\sqrt{gL}=0.8819\sqrt{gL}$$

Check with (c): constant $\ddot s=\tfrac23g$ from rest gives $\dot s^2=2\ddot sL=\tfrac43gL$. The time to slide $L$ is $\sqrt{2L/\ddot s}=\sqrt{3L/g}$ and the wedge has moved $\Delta X=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}L=0.2887\,L$ towards $+x$.

#### Step 5. Work of the reaction on each body

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x: Kinetic energy theorem for $P$ alone: $\tfrac12m|\mathbf v_P|^2=W_{weight}+W_{N\to P}$ with $W_{weight}=\tfrac12mgL$: $W_{N\to P}=\tfrac7{18}mgL-\tfrac9{18}mgL=-\tfrac19mgL$. For the wedge: $W_{-N\to wedge}=\tfrac12(2m)\dot X^2=\tfrac19mgL$. The reaction **does** work on each body (the incline moves), but the two works cancel: energy is transferred from $P$ to the wedge.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x: Show that $P$ moves along a straight line in $S_0$ and find the angle $\beta$ of this line with the horizontal. Compare it with $\alpha$ for $\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- $\tan\beta=\dfrac{\ddot s\sin\alpha}{\ddot s\cos\alpha-\ddot X}=\Big(1+\dfrac mM\Big)\tan\alpha$.
- $\alpha=30^\circ$, $M=2m$: $\tan\beta=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\beta=40.89^\circ>\alpha$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
#### Step 1. A straight path

$\mathbf a_P=\ddot X\,\mathbf i+\ddot s\,\mathbf u$ is a constant vector (part (c)). Integrating twice from rest (Barrow): $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf a_P\,t$ and $\mathbf r_P-\mathbf r_P(0)=\tfrac12\mathbf a_P\,t^2$, so $P$ moves along the fixed straight line through its initial position with direction $\mathbf a_P$.

#### Step 2. Its slope

In Cartesian components $\mathbf a_P=(\ddot X-\ddot s\cos\alpha)\,\mathbf i-\ddot s\sin\alpha\,\mathbf j$; the line descends towards $-x$ with

$$\tan\beta=\frac{\ddot s\sin\alpha}{\ddot s\cos\alpha-\ddot X}=\frac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha-\dfrac{\ddot X}{\ddot s}}$$

From (c), $\dfrac{\ddot X}{\ddot s}=\dfrac{m\cos\alpha}{M+m}$ (the same ratio as $\dot X/\dot s$ in (e)), so $\cos\alpha-\dfrac{m\cos\alpha}{M+m}=\dfrac{M\cos\alpha}{M+m}$ and

$$\tan\beta=\frac{(M+m)\sin\alpha}{M\cos\alpha}=\Big(1+\frac mM\Big)\tan\alpha$$

#### Step 3. Numbers

$\tan\beta=\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac1{\sqrt3}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=0.8660$, $\beta=40.89^\circ$. The particle descends **more steeply** than the incline, because the incline recedes under it. Check with (e): $|v_{Py}|/|v_{Px}|=\sqrt{gL/3}\big/\tfrac23\sqrt{gL}=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$.

chunks.t: Particle on a free wedge: a moving constraint, the reaction, momentum and energy, and the limit of a massless
chunks.x:
- **Dimensional check:** $\ddot X$ and $\ddot s$ are $g$ times a ratio of masses times trigonometric factors (m s$^{-2}$); $N=Mmg\cos\alpha/(M+m\sin^2\alpha)$ is kg$\cdot$m s$^{-2}$ = N; $\dot s^2=\tfrac43gL$ is m$^2$s$^{-2}$; the works are $mgL$ times numbers (J).
- **Limiting cases:** $M\to\infty$ recovers the fixed incline ($\beta\to\alpha$); $M\to0$ gives free fall ($\beta\to90^\circ$, $\tan\beta\to\infty$); $\alpha\to0$ gives $\ddot X=\ddot s=0$, $N=mg$ (nothing moves); $\alpha\to\pi/2$ gives $N\to0$, $\ddot X\to0$, $\ddot s\to g$ (the particle falls along the vertical face).
- **Common mistakes in the exam:** (1) using $N=mg\cos\alpha$ as on a fixed incline; (2) forgetting the inertia force $-m\ddot X\,\mathbf i$ in $S_1$, or giving it the wrong sign; (3) writing energy conservation for $P$ alone (the reaction works on $P$: $-\tfrac19mgL$ here); (4) assuming the particle's absolute path is parallel to the incline.

chunks.x:
The bank behind the Extra problems pages (1st Midterm: Concepts and Problems) and the Exam simulator of the portal. Each line is one note in this folder; `python tools/build_mechanics_bank.py` turns them into `subjects/engineering-mechanics/data/problems.json` and the two pages. What is official and what is practice
None of these items is an official exercise. They are written for the portal in the style of the Midterm 1 papers (2011 to 2024) and of the true/false questions of the finals. The structure analysis is in `docs/midterm1_blueprint.md`.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
For the letter T, we first consider a frame $S_0$, whose $y$ axis is the vertical symmetric line and the $x$ axis coincides with the bottom line of the upper rectangle. The center of mass is located in $S_0$ as

$$\mathbf{r}_0^G = \frac{wt - (h-t)^2}{2(w+h-t)}\,\mathbf{j}.$$

In the frame with origin on $G$, we have

$$I_{Gx} = \frac{\sigma}{3}\left[wt^3 + (h-t)^3 t\right] - mr^2, \quad r = -\frac{wt - (h-t)^2}{2(w+h-t)},$$

$$I_{Gy} = \frac{\sigma t}{12}\left[w^3 + (h-t)t^2\right].$$

The product of inertia $P_{xz,yz}$ is zero.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
Mordor ($\mathcal{M}$) exerts a force on The Ring ($\mathcal{R}$) that can be written as:

$$ \boldsymbol{F}_{\mathcal{M}} = \int_{\mathcal{R}} \beta \boldsymbol{r}_0^P \, dm = \beta \boldsymbol{r}_0^G M . $$

The moment exerted by Mordor on The Ring about G can be written as:

$$ \boldsymbol{M}_{G_{\mathcal{M}}} = \int_{\mathcal{R}} \boldsymbol{r}_B^P \times \beta \boldsymbol{r}_0^P \, dm = \beta \int_{\mathcal{R}} \boldsymbol{r}_B^P \times \left(\boldsymbol{r}_0^G + \boldsymbol{r}_B^P\right) dm = \beta \int_{\mathcal{R}} \boldsymbol{r}_B^P \times \boldsymbol{r}_0^G \, dm = \beta \int_{\mathcal{R}} \boldsymbol{r}_B^P \, dm \times \boldsymbol{r}_0^G = 0 . $$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
The EOM for 2 DOF are

$$ m\ddot{y}_G = -mg - k\left(y_G + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,a\cos\theta}{3}\right) , $$

$$ ma\ddot{\theta} = 4\sqrt{3}\,k\left(y_G\sin\theta + 2a\cos\theta\right) . $$

The equation to solve the reaction force from the vertical line $R$ (defined positive in $\boldsymbol{i}$ direction) is

$$ R = ak\left(2 - \frac{\sqrt{3}\sin\theta}{3}\right) . $$

The 4 initial conditions required to solve the EOM are

$$ t = 0 \rightarrow y_G = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{6} , \quad \dot{y}_G = v_0, \quad \theta = 0, \quad \dot{\theta} = -\frac{\sqrt{3}\,u_0}{a} . $$

At equilibrium for $\theta = \pi/4$, we have

$$ y_G = -2a , \quad k = \frac{mg}{a\left(2 - \sqrt{6}/6\right)} , \quad R = ka\left(2 - \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\right) . $$

After fixing the position of G, the linearized EOM for the perturbation $\phi$

$$ \ddot{\phi} + \frac{8\sqrt{6}\,k}{m}\phi = 0 , $$

which is a harmonic oscillator with the natural frequency being $\Omega = \sqrt{8\sqrt{6}\,k/m}$ .

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x: The vector basis $B_1\{\mathbf{i}_1, \mathbf{j}_1, \mathbf{k}_1\}$ is defined as: $\mathbf{k}_1 \parallel \mathbf{k}$; $\mathbf{i}_1$ is parallel to the perpendicular axis of the disk, from the axis $Oz$ to the disc; $\mathbf{j}_1 = \mathbf{k}_1 \times \mathbf{i}_1$. The angular velocity and acceleration of the disk is $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{B0} = \omega(-\mathbf{i}_1 + \mathbf{k}_1)$ and $\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{B0} = -\omega^2\mathbf{j}_1$. The acceleration of the contact point $C$ is $\mathbf{a}_0^{C(B)} = \omega^2 R(\mathbf{i}_1 + \mathbf{k}_1)$.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
For $\mu = 0$,

$$6\dot{x} + \dot{\theta}R\sin\theta = 6\omega R \quad , \quad 24\dot{x}^2 + 13\dot{\theta}^2R^2 + 8\dot{x}\dot{\theta}R\sin\theta - 8gR\sin\theta = 37\omega^2R^2$$

For $\mu \to \infty$,

$$\dot{\theta}^2R(37 - 8\sin\theta) - 8g\sin\theta = 37\omega^2R \ .$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
The only forces that appear on the fork-disc system arise from the collar joint and the weight of both disk and fork. From the equations of motion in basis $B_2$ it can be noticed that for the disk alone the angular momentum with respect to $\boldsymbol{i}_2$ is conserved. Therefore, one of the quadratures of the problem is:

$$\dot{\phi} = C_1. \tag{7}$$

Furthermore, mechanical energy is conserved due to the fact that $(i)$ the resultant reaction force at the collar does not work since $\boldsymbol{F}\cdot\boldsymbol{v}_0^{O_1} = 0$, and $(ii)$ because the resultant torque has no component along the direction of $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{21}$, the resultant reaction torque does not work either. $(iii)$ Last but not least the other forces present are the disk and fork respective weights, which are conservative forces.

This provide with the following conservation law:

$$\dot{\theta}^2\left(\frac{I_2}{2} + \frac{mR^2}{8} + \frac{mb^2}{2}\right) + \dot{\phi}^2\left(\frac{mR^2}{4}\right) - (mb + Ma)\,g\cos\theta = C_2. \tag{8}$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
The resultant reaction force and torque that the axis $AB$ applies on the fork-disc system at $O_1$ is $\boldsymbol{R}_{O_1} = \left[\ddot{\theta}\,(Ma + mb) + g\sin\theta\,(M + m)\right]\boldsymbol{i}_2 - \left[\dot{\theta}^2\,(Ma + mb) + g\cos\theta\,(M + m)\right]\boldsymbol{k}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}_{O_1} = -\dfrac{mR^2}{2}\dot{\phi}\dot{\theta}\boldsymbol{k}_2$, respectively.

The resultant (internal) reaction force and torque that the axis $CD$ applies on the disk at $O$ is $\boldsymbol{R}_O = \left(mb\ddot{\theta} + mg\sin\theta\right)\boldsymbol{i}_2 - \left(mb\dot{\theta}^2 + mg\cos\theta\right)\boldsymbol{k}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}_O = \dfrac{mR^2}{4}\ddot{\theta}\boldsymbol{j}_2 - \dfrac{mR^2}{2}\dot{\phi}\dot{\theta}\boldsymbol{k}_2$, respectively.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
We define $\xi = \dot x_G$, $\eta = \dot y_G$, $\boldsymbol\omega_{B0} = \omega_x\mathbf i + \omega_y\mathbf j + \omega_z\mathbf k$.

For rolling with slip, there are 5 DOF. The EOM are

$$\dot\xi = \frac{-\mu g(\xi - a\omega_y)}{\sqrt{(\xi - a\omega_y)^2 + (\eta + a\omega_x)^2}} \quad , \quad \dot\eta = \frac{-\mu g(\eta + a\omega_x)}{\sqrt{(\xi - a\omega_y)^2 + (\eta + a\omega_x)^2}} \quad ,$$

$$2a\dot\omega_x = 5\dot\eta \quad , \quad 2a\dot\omega_y = -5\dot\xi \quad , \quad \dot\omega_z = 0 \quad .$$

For rolling without slip, there are 3 DOF. The problem can be reduced to quadratures as

$$\xi = a\omega_y = C_1 \quad , \quad \eta = -a\omega_x = C_2 \quad , \quad \omega_z = C_3 \quad ,$$

with the constants to be determined by IC.

The ball hits the pocket with velocity and angular velocity being

$$\mathbf v_0^G = \frac{2\xi_0}{\sqrt 5}\,\mathbf i \quad , \quad \boldsymbol\omega_{B0} = \frac{\xi_0}{a}\left(\frac{11}{4} - \sqrt 5\right)\mathbf j \quad .$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
The length $L$ required to achieve the final angular velocity $\omega_f$ is

$$L^2 = \frac{(I + mR^2)(\omega_0 - \omega_f)}{m(\omega_0 + \omega_f)} \quad .$$

The tension is

$$T = \frac{2KI\omega_0^3 t}{R\left(1 + K\omega_0^2 t^2\right)^2} \quad , \quad \text{with} \quad K = \frac{mR^2}{I + mR^2} \quad .$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
This problem has 4 DOF. To solve the motion of the cylinder, it requires 8 equations to solve for the 8 *unknowns* $x_G$, $y_G$, $z_G$, $\beta$, $\theta$, $\varphi$, $T_C$, and $T_D$. In this case, the *unknown coordinates* have to be solved together with the *unknown reaction forces*. The constraint equations can not be decoupled from the Newton ordinary differential equations.

$$ (\cos\theta\cos\beta - x_G/l)^2 + (\cos\theta\sin\beta - y_G/l)^2 + (\sin\theta + z_G/l)^2 = 1 $$

$$ (\cos\theta\cos\beta + x_G/l)^2 + (3 - \cos\theta\sin\beta - y_G/l)^2 + (\sin\theta - z_G/l)^2 = 1 $$

$$ T\boldsymbol{i} : m\ddot{x}_G = (T_C - T_D)\cos\theta\cos\beta - (T_C + T_D)x_G/l $$

$$ T\boldsymbol{j} : m\ddot{y}_G = (T_C - T_D)\cos\theta\sin\beta - (T_C + T_D)y_G/l + 3T_D $$

$$ T\boldsymbol{k} : m\ddot{z}_G = -mg + (T_D - T_C)\sin\theta - (T_C + T_D)z_G/l $$

$$ R\boldsymbol{i}_2 : \ddot{\varphi} - \ddot{\beta}\sin\theta - \dot{\beta}\dot{\theta}\cos\theta = 0 \rightarrow \dot{\varphi} - \dot{\beta}\sin\theta = \text{const.} $$

$$ \begin{aligned} R\boldsymbol{j}_2 : ml^2\left[\ddot{\theta}\mu - \dot{\beta}^2(\lambda - \mu)\cos\theta\sin\theta + \dot{\beta}\dot{\varphi}\lambda\cos\theta\right] &= (T_D - T_C)\left(x_G\sin\theta\cos\beta + y_G\sin\theta\sin\beta + z_G\cos\theta\right) - 3T_D l\sin\theta\sin\beta \end{aligned} $$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
$$ \begin{aligned} R\boldsymbol{k}_2 : ml^2\left[\ddot{\beta}\mu\cos\theta - \dot{\beta}\dot{\theta}(2\mu - \lambda)\sin\theta - \dot{\theta}\dot{\varphi}\lambda\right] &= (T_D - T_C)\left(x_G\sin\beta - y_G\cos\beta\right) + 3T_D l\cos\beta \end{aligned} $$

If the body-fixed vector basis is used to decompose the equations for rotation, it leads to:

$$ \begin{aligned} ml^2\lambda\alpha_{x_B} &= 0 \quad \Rightarrow \dot{\beta}\sin\theta - \dot{\varphi} = \text{const} \\ ml^2\mu\alpha_{y_B} - ml^2(\mu - \lambda)\omega_{x_B}\omega_{z_B} &= -(T_1 - T_2)\left[x_G(\cos\beta\sin\theta\cos\varphi + \sin\beta\sin\varphi) + y_G(\sin\beta\sin\theta\cos\varphi - \cos\beta\sin\varphi) + z_G\cos\theta\cos\varphi\right] - 3T_2 l(\sin\beta\sin\theta\cos\varphi - \cos\beta\sin\varphi) \\ ml^2\mu\alpha_{z_B} + ml^2(\mu - \lambda)\omega_{x_B}\omega_{y_B} &= (T_1 - T_2)\left[x_G(\cos\beta\sin\theta\sin\varphi - \sin\beta\cos\varphi) + y_G(\sin\beta\sin\theta\sin\varphi + \cos\beta\cos\varphi) + z_G\cos\theta\sin\varphi\right] + 3T_2 l(\sin\beta\sin\theta\sin\varphi + \cos\beta\cos\varphi) , \end{aligned} $$

with $T_1 = T_C$ and $T_2 = T_D$. Conservation of mechanical energy gives

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x: $$ \frac{m}{2}\left(\dot{x}_G^2 + \dot{y}_G^2 + \dot{z}_G^2\right) + \frac{ml^2}{2}\left[\lambda\left(\dot{\varphi} - \dot{\beta}\sin\theta\right)^2 + \mu\dot{\theta}^2 + \mu\left(\dot{\beta}\cos\theta\right)^2\right] + mgz_G = \text{const.} $$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
The EOM of the system is

$$\frac{425}{64}\,md^2\dot\theta^2 + 5mg\,\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{4}\,d(1-\sin\theta) = 5mg\,\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{4}\,d\,.$$

There are two equilibrium positions, given by $\theta = \pi/2$ and $\theta = -\pi/2$. After expanding about the stable equilibrium $\theta = \pi/2$ as $\theta = \pi/2 + \delta$ with $\delta \ll 1$, the EOM reads:

$$\frac{425}{64}\,md^2\dot\delta^2 + 5mg\,\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{4}\,\frac{d\delta^2}{2} = E\,,$$

whose angular frequency is

$$\sqrt{\frac{8g}{85d}\left(\sqrt{2}-1\right)}$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
Vector $\mathbf i_1$ is $\mathbf{OG}$ and $\mathbf j_1$ is calculated following the right-hand rule so that $\mathbf k = \mathbf k_1$. Two equations come from projecting Newton's second law along $\mathbf i_1$ and $\mathbf j_1$ so that:

$$-2m\left[\ddot\xi + \dot\theta^2(4L-\xi)\right] = 2mg\cos\theta - k\left[4L-\xi-L\sin(\phi-\theta)-2L\sin\theta\right] - T,$$

$$2m\left[\ddot\theta(4L-\xi) - 2\dot\xi\dot\theta\right] = -2mg\sin\theta - k\left[L\cos(\phi-\theta)-2L\cos\theta\right].$$

Tension can be eliminated using Newton's second law for particle P in the $\mathbf j$ direction:

$$-m\ddot\xi = -mg + T,$$

The third equation is the equation of angular momentum of the block at G about $\mathbf k$. The moment of inertia of the block at G about $\mathbf k$ is $I^G_z = 5mL^2/6$. Only the spring causes a torque about G, so:

$$\frac{5mL^2\ddot\phi}{6} = kL\left[(4L-\xi)\cos(\phi-\theta) - 2L\sin\phi\right] \qquad (9)$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
The smaller wheel will leave the ground when the normal at $P$ is $N_P = 0$. Imposing this condition on the first rotational equation, using the rest of equations to reduce the problem to an equation on $N_P$ and $\dot\psi$,

$$\frac{10(A+3B)}{ma^2}\sqrt{3}\,\dot\psi^2/4 + 9\sqrt{3}\left(27\dot\psi^2/10\right) = 13\,\frac{g}{a} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \dot\psi^2_{\max} = \frac{104g}{323\sqrt{3}\,a}$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Rigid Body Official Key
chunks.x:
To obtain the force $\mathbf{F}$ we use the equation of motion of the particle:

$$m\mathbf{a}_0^P = -mg[\sin\gamma\,\mathbf{i}_0 + \cos\gamma\,\mathbf{j}_0] - \mathbf{F}.$$

Hence,

$$\mathbf{F} = -mg[\sin\gamma\,\mathbf{i}_0 + \cos\gamma\,\mathbf{j}_0] - m\mathbf{a}_0^P.$$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.h: 📝 Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics - Problem Statements
chunks.x:
Official problem statements from the UC3M Aerospace Engineering problem collection (`Problems.pdf`, Chapter 1). These problems test kinematics in Cartesian, Cylindrical, and Frenet-Serret intrinsic bases, curvature, and relative motion between points.

**Status:** Verbatim problem statements transcribed faithfully from official department exams and problem sets.

Complete Analytical Solutions Ready
All 6 problems have full, step-by-step pedagogical solutions developed in: Solution Set - Topic 1 Particle Kinematics.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.x:
An out-of-control rocket traces an upward helical trajectory described in Cartesian coordinates for $t > 0$ by:

$$ x = a\cos(\omega t) \tag{1} $$
$$ y = a\sin(\omega t) \tag{2} $$
$$ z = v_z t \tag{3} $$

where $a$, $v_z$, and $\omega$ are constants.

*Figure: Helical trajectory with position r(t), the Cartesian basis i, j, k, the cylindrical basis e_R, e_theta, e_z and the intrinsic basis e_t, e_n, e_b (taken from MIT OCW) Source: Problems.pdf, p. 6.*

* **(a)** Express the position, velocity, and acceleration vectors in the Cartesian $x, y, z$ system using unit vectors $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$.
* **(b)** Express the position, velocity, and acceleration vectors in the cylindrical coordinate system using unit vectors $\mathbf{e}_R, \mathbf{e}_\theta, \mathbf{e}_z$.
* **(c)** Express the velocity and acceleration vectors using $s, \rho$ and the vector basis $\mathbf{e}_t, \mathbf{e}_n, \mathbf{e}_b$.
* **(d)** Compute the modulus of the velocity vector.
* **(e)** Express the evolution of the arc-length coordinate as a function of time.
* **(f)** Write down the trajectory as a function of the arc-length coordinate.
* **(g)** Where is the center of curvature for this curve when the particle is located at $(x, y, z) = (a, 0, 0)$?

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.x:
A planar spiral is given by the equation $r = \alpha e^{\beta\theta}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants, $r$ is the radial coordinate, and $\theta$ is the angular coordinate. If a particle moves along the spiral according to the equation $\theta = \delta t^n$ (where $\delta$ is a constant), determine:

* **(a)** The radial and transverse components of the velocity.
* **(b)** The radial and transverse components of the acceleration.
* **(c)** The tangential and normal components of the velocity.
* **(d)** The tangential and normal components of the acceleration.
* **(e)** The radius of curvature of the spiral.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.x:
A point particle describes the astroid:

$$ x = a\cos^3\phi, \qquad y = a\sin^3\phi $$

with a motion whose tangential acceleration is constant, $k$. If the point is initially at rest at $\phi = 0$, compute the evolution of the position as a function of time while the particle is in one of the smooth segments of the astroid. *(Hint: $ds = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}$)*.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.x:
An aircraft moves at constant altitude $y_0$ with velocity $v_0$ in the $x$ direction. At time $t = 0$ it is located at $x = 0$, and it begins to accelerate in the $x$ direction at a constant rate $a_x$. Describe the position, velocity, and acceleration in polar coordinates $r, \theta$, and answer the following questions:

* **(a)** Show that: $\dot{r} = \frac{v(t) x(t)}{r(t)}$
* **(b)** Show that: $\dot{\theta} = -\frac{v(t) y_0}{r^2(t)}$
* **(c)** Show that: $\ddot{r} = \frac{v^2(t) y_0^2 + a_x x(t) r^2(t)}{r^3(t)}$
* **(d)** Show that: $\ddot{\theta} = y_0\frac{2v^2(t) x(t) - a_x r^2(t)}{r^4(t)}$

From these expressions form the acceleration vector $\mathbf{a} = a_r\mathbf{e}_r + a_\theta\mathbf{e}_\theta$. Repeat the problem using Cartesian coordinates.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.x: An airplane $A$ is flying horizontally with a constant speed $v_A$, and is towing a glider $B$. The glider is gaining altitude. The tow cable has a length $r$, and the angle $\theta$ formed between the tow cable and the horizontal is increasing at a constant rate of $\dot{\theta}$. We want to determine the magnitude of the velocity, $v_B^0$, and the acceleration, $a_B^0$, of the glider as a function of $\theta$ and its derivatives.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 1: Fundamentals and Particle Kinematics
chunks.x:
A point particle $P$ travels along a curve given by:

$$ y = \sin x $$

with a velocity along $x$ given by $\dot{x} = 1$.

* **(a)** Find the intrinsic, unitary vector basis associated to the curve.
* **(b)** Express $x$ as a function of an arc length parameter, $s$. You can leave your solution as a function of an integral.
* **(c)** Find the tangent and normal acceleration components of $P$ as a function of $x$.
* **(d)** Write the radius of curvature of the trajectory as a function of $x$.

chunks.h: 📝 Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics - Problem Statements
chunks.x:
Official problem statements from the UC3M Aerospace Engineering problem collection (`Problems.pdf`, Chapter 1). These problems test Newton's second law, linear momentum, kinetic energy, work, conservative forces, potential energy, 1D energy landscapes, aerodynamic drag, and the simple pendulum.

**Status:** Verbatim problem statements transcribed faithfully from official department exams and problem sets.

Complete Analytical Solutions Ready
All 10 problems have full, step-by-step pedagogical solutions developed in: Solution Set - Topic 2 Point Particle Dynamics.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.h: 📌 Problem 10: Conservative Force and Potential I
chunks.x: A particle of mass $m$ moves under a force $\mathbf{F} = -c x^3\mathbf{i}$, where $c$ is a positive constant. Find the potential energy function. If the particle starts from rest at $x = -a$, what is its velocity when it reaches $x = 0$? In the subsequent motion, where does it stop again?

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.h: 📌 Problem 11: Conservative Force and Potential II
chunks.x:
The potential energy function of a particle of mass $m$ is:

$$ V(x) = -\frac{c}{2}(x^2 - a^2)^2 $$

where $c$ and $a$ are positive constants. Sketch this function, and describe the possible types of motion in the three cases:

* **(a)** $E > 0$
* **(b)** $E < -\frac{ca^4}{2}$
* **(c)** $-\frac{ca^4}{2} < E < 0$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.h: 📌 Problem 12: Conservative Force and Potential III
chunks.x:
A particle moving under a conservative force oscillates between $x_1$ and $x_2$. Show that the period of oscillation is:

$$ \tau = 2\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \sqrt{\frac{m}{2[V(x_2) - V(x)]}}\,dx $$

where $V(x)$ is the potential energy function. In particular, if $V(x) = \frac{1}{2}m\omega_0^2(x^2 - bx^4)$, show that the period for oscillations of amplitude $a$ is:

$$ \tau = \frac{2}{\omega_0}\int_{-a}^a \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\sqrt{1 - b(a^2 + x^2)}} $$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.h: 📌 Problem 13: Conservative Force and Potential IV
chunks.x:
A particle of mass $m$ moves along the $Ox$ axis under the potential:

$$ V(x) = mgx\left[\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 - 3\right] $$

Compute the evolution of the particle as a function of time, when it is released from $x_0 = a$ with an initial velocity $v_0 = \sqrt{8ga}$ directed along the positive $Ox$ axis.

*(Tip: $\int \frac{dx}{(x+1)\sqrt{2-x}} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\text{arctanh}\left(\sqrt{\frac{2-x}{3}}\right)$)*.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.h: 📌 Problem 14: Conservative Force and Potential V
chunks.x: A particle of mass $m$ is moving along the $Ox$ axis under the force $\mathbf{F}(x) = mK x e^{x/a}\mathbf{i}$, where $K$ and $a$ are known positive constants. The initial position of the particle is $x = a$ and the initial velocity is $\mathbf{v} = -v_0\mathbf{i}$. Describe the possible types of motion of the particle as a function of $v_0$.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.h: 📌 Problem 15: Stokes Drag and Terminal Velocity
chunks.x:
The Stokes' law states that the magnitude of the drag force acting on a sphere of radius $r$ and velocity $v$ moving on a fluid at rest of dynamic viscosity $\mu$ is: $F(v) = 6\pi\mu rv$. Assuming the density of a vertically-falling sphere is twice the density of the fluid ($\rho_0$), and considering drag, the weight, and the buoyancy of the sphere, compute:

* **(a)** The terminal velocity of the sphere.
* **(b)** The evolution of the position as a function of time, if the sphere starts from rest.

Remember that the kinematic viscosity is defined as $\nu = \mu / \rho_0$.

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.x:
A football has frontal surface area $S$, mass $m$, and a drag coefficient $C_D$. It falls vertically through the air of density $\rho$. It is assumed that the forces acting on the ball are only gravity and drag. The drag can be modeled as: $D = \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 S C_D$, with $v$ the speed of the ball. Compute its terminal speed and its position as a function of time.

You may find the following integrals useful:

$$ \int \frac{dx}{x_0^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{x_0}\text{atanh}\left(\frac{x}{x_0}\right); \qquad \int \tanh x\,dx = \ln\cosh x $$

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.x:
A force attracts a heavy particle $M$ of mass $m$ to a point $O$. The attractive force is proportional to the mass of the particle and to the distance $OM$. The proportionality coefficient is $k^2$. The coordinate system $Oxyz$ has the origin at the centre of attraction $O$ and the axis $Oz$ is vertically oriented. Initially, the coordinates of $M$ are:

$$ (x_0, y_0, z_0) = \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}g}{k^2}, 0, 0\right) $$

and its initial velocity is:

$$ (\dot{x}_0, \dot{y}_0, \dot{z}_0) = \left(0, \frac{2g}{k}, 0\right) $$

* **(a)** Describe the motion of $M$, specifying clearly the shape of the path.
* **(b)** What is the velocity of the particle as a function of $t$?

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.x:
To understand the vibrations that occur in a turbojet when the mass distribution of the rotor is slightly unbalanced, we can consider the turbojet as a rigid disk of mass $m$ that rotates at a fixed angular velocity $\omega$, with the center of mass $G$ being separated from the geometric center $C$ by a fixed distance [called $\ell$ in the figure]. An elastic restoring force (with constant $k$) tries to keep $C$ at its design position $O$. We call $x_0^G, y_0^G$ the Cartesian coordinates of $G$, and $x_0^C, y_0^C$ the Cartesian coordinates of $C$. Considering the weight of the disk negligible, write down the equation of the dynamics of $G$. Assuming that the homogeneous solution is damped over time and only the particular solution remains, write down the expression of $x_0^G(t)$ and $x_0^C(t)$. Can we affirm that $|\boldsymbol{OC}| > |\boldsymbol{OG}|$ if $\omega > \sqrt{k/m}$?

*Figure: Rotating disk of centre C with the centre of mass G at distance l, angle omega t from the x direction, spring k from O to C, axes Oxy Source: Problems.pdf, p. 31.*

chunks.t: Problem Set - Topic 2: Point Particle Dynamics
chunks.x:
An airplane is taxiing over a bumpy runway of vertical profile $y_1 = \sin(x)$ with a horizontal velocity $c$. The vertical motion of the airplane can be modeled as that of a heavy particle $P$ of mass $m$ supported on a landing gear of nominal length $L$ when unloaded. Consider that the landing gear has stiffness constant $k$ and negligible damping.

*Figure: Mass m on a spring k whose lower end follows the bumpy runway profile y1 = sin x Source: Problems.pdf, p. 31.*

* **(a)** At what taxiing speed is the system in resonance with the bumpy road?
* **(b)** Find the expression of the amplitude of the airplane oscillations when the taxiing velocity $c$ is very high. Hint: the expression depends on $c$.
* **(c)** Consider now that the landing gear has damping constant $\lambda$. How does the results above change? Consider the underdamped, critical, and overdamped cases. What value of $\lambda$ would you choose for this application and why? If the mass of the aircraft changes (e.g. more or less payload), does this affect your conclusion?
